HCC pilot — random-effect vs interaction tissue formula

V1_nk liver baseline sanity check on 4 TIMES biomarkers

Author
Affiliation

Chen Zhan

SAiGENCI, The University of Adelaide

Published

06 Jul 2026

Abstract

Pilot comparison of the production posteriorHCA V1_nk brms formula — which treats tissue-specific covariate slopes as random effects — against a fixed interaction alternative where age, sex and ethnicity interact with tissue_groups. We focus on the comprehensive healthy liver NK baseline used in the TIMES HCC case study, fit interaction models for four atlas-covered biomarkers (SPON2, ZFP36L2, ZFP36, VIM), and ask whether the interaction parameterisation is more stable or more concordant for liver (n = 71) than partial pooling from blood-dominated training data. We then project the four TIMES HCC cohorts (IF/TC x REC/non-REC) onto both baselines and ask which formula better serves the case study — i.e. which one preserves the expected ordering that recurrent cohorts sit farther from the healthy liver NK reference than non-recurrent cohorts.

Motivation

The TIMES HCC case study uses a comprehensive healthy liver NK baseline from the posteriorHCA V1_nk atlas. Each gene is modelled as a zero-inflated negative binomial regression on pseudobulk counts with rich covariate structure. In production, tissue-specific deviations enter as random effects:

\[ \texttt{(1 + age\_decade * sex + ethnicity\_groups | tissue\_groups)} \]

This partial pooling is attractive when many tissues contribute information, but liver contributes only 71 of 3,226 NK pseudobulk samples (2.2%), while blood contributes 74%. A concern for the HCC application is that liver tissue effects — and liver-specific age/sex/ethnicity slopes — may be shrunk toward the blood-dominated population mean, appearing as if liver biology is embedded in the global fixed effect rather than estimated independently.

An alternative is to replace the random-slopes tissue term with fixed interactions:

\[ \texttt{age\_decade:tissue\_groups + sex:tissue\_groups + ...} \]

This removes hierarchical shrinkage: liver coefficients are estimated only from liver rows. The trade-off is a much larger parameter space and potential instability when liver sample size is modest.

This report is a pilot on four TIMES biomarkers present in the V1_nk store. It does not re-fit the production random-effect models (those are loaded from the targets store); it does fit the interaction alternative on the login node and saves all artefacts under params$out_dir.

Formulas compared

Production random-effect model

Code 
source(file.path(params$case_dir, "R", "re_vs_interaction_helpers.R"))
spec_re <- formula_re_spec()
spec_int <- formula_interaction_spec()

knitr::kable(data.frame(
  component = c("counts", "shape"),
  formula = c(spec_re$counts, spec_re$shape)
))
component formula
counts counts ~ 1 + offset(offset) + age_decade * sex + disease_groups_altered + ethnicity_groups + assay_groups_altered + (1 | dataset_id_altered) + (1 + age_decade * sex + ethnicity_groups | tissue_groups)
shape shape ~ 1 + disease_groups_altered + assay_groups_altered + ethnicity_groups + (1 | tissue_groups)

Interaction pilot model

The interaction formula is the fixed-effect expansion of the random-slopes structure inside tissue_groups. Global age_decade * sex fixed terms from the RE model are absorbed into tissue-specific interaction terms.

Code 
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  component = c("counts", "shape"),
  formula = c(spec_int$counts, spec_int$shape)
))
component formula
counts counts ~ 1 + offset(offset) + disease_groups_altered + assay_groups_altered + (1 | dataset_id_altered) + tissue_groups + age_decade:tissue_groups + sex:tissue_groups + age_decade:sex:tissue_groups + ethnicity_groups:tissue_groups
shape shape ~ 1 + disease_groups_altered + assay_groups_altered + ethnicity_groups + tissue_groups

Fit interaction models and compare baselines

Interaction brms fits are pre-computed and cached as fit_interaction_<GENE>.rds. Set params$refresh_fits: true to refit. Comparison tables and posterior baseline draws are written alongside the fits.

Code 
if (isTRUE(params$refresh_fits) ||
    !file.exists(file.path(params$out_dir, "baseline_comparison_4genes.csv"))) {
  suppressPackageStartupMessages({
    library(targets)
    library(brms)
    library(posterior)
    library(SummarizedExperiment)
  })
  pilot <- run_re_vs_interaction_pilot(
    case_dir = params$case_dir,
    out_dir = params$out_dir,
    model_store_root = params$model_store_root,
    target_cell_type = params$target_cell_type,
    baseline_tissue = params$baseline_tissue_group,
    n_draws = params$n_posterior_draws,
    refresh_fits = isTRUE(params$refresh_fits)
  )
  comparison <- pilot$comparison
  draws_df <- pilot$draws
} else {
  comparison <- read_csv(
    file.path(params$out_dir, "baseline_comparison_4genes.csv"),
    show_col_types = FALSE
  )
  draws_df <- read_csv(
    file.path(params$out_dir, "baseline_draws_long.csv"),
    show_col_types = FALSE
  )
}

Comprehensive liver baseline comparison

For each gene we compute the same comprehensive healthy liver baseline used in the universal HCC case study:

  • disease_groups_altered = Normal
  • tissue_groups = liver
  • offset = 0
  • marginalised over the full atlas grid of sex × age_decade × ethnicity × assay
  • posterior_linpred(transform = FALSE) then averaged across grid rows per draw
Code 
comparison |>
  mutate(
    across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)),
    fold_median_mu = median_mu_int / median_mu_re
  ) |>
  select(
    gene, mean_log_mu_re, mean_log_mu_int, diff_mean_log_mu,
    sd_log_mu_re, sd_log_mu_int, corr_draws, rmse_draws,
    median_mu_re, median_mu_int, fold_median_mu,
    max_rhat_re, max_rhat_int, n_liver_rows
  )

HCC cohort projection onto both baselines

The point of the baseline is to serve the TIMES HCC case study. We therefore project the four HCC cohorts (IF/TC x REC/non-REC) onto both baseline formulas and ask which one better matches the case-study expectation. Cohort log(μ) values are the edgeR NB estimates at offset = 0 produced by the universal-baseline report and are independent of the atlas formula, so the same cohort projections can be overlaid on either baseline density.

Code 
model_labels <- c(random_effect = "Random effect", interaction = "Interaction")

cohort_tests <- read_csv(params$cohort_results_csv, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(gene, cohort, compartment, recurrence, cohort_log_mu, cohort_se) |>
  filter(gene %in% unique(draws_df$gene))

Baseline densities per gene, with HCC cohorts

For each gene we plot the posterior log(μ) density of both baselines (random-effect vs interaction) and overlay the four HCC cohort projections as vertical lines — the direct analogue of the universal case-study figure, split by model formula.

Code 
model_colours <- c(`Random effect` = "#4DBBD5", Interaction = "#E64B35")
cohort_colours <- c(
  IF_REC = "#C23B4A",
  IF_non_REC = "#2878B5",
  TC_REC = "#E08A2E",
  TC_non_REC = "#2D8B57"
)

draws_plot <- draws_df |>
  mutate(
    model = recode(model, !!!model_labels),
    model = factor(model, levels = c("Random effect", "Interaction"))
  )

cohort_plot <- cohort_tests |>
  mutate(cohort = factor(cohort, levels = names(cohort_colours)))

ggplot() +
  geom_density(
    data = draws_plot,
    aes(x = baseline_log_mu, fill = model),
    colour = NA,
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    data = cohort_plot,
    aes(xintercept = cohort_log_mu, colour = cohort),
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = model_colours) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = cohort_colours) +
  facet_wrap(~ gene, scales = "free", ncol = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Healthy liver NK baseline by model formula, with HCC cohorts",
    subtitle = "Filled densities = posterior baseline log(mu) per formula; lines = edgeR cohort log(mu) at offset 0",
    x = "log(mu)",
    y = "Density",
    fill = "Baseline formula",
    colour = "HCC cohort"
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

Which baseline serves the case study?

The case study expects recurrent (REC) cohorts to sit farther from the healthy liver NK reference than non-recurrent (non-REC) cohorts. We quantify each cohort’s distance from each baseline as a standardized deviation z = (cohort log(μ) − baseline mean log(μ)) / baseline SD, then compare the absolute distance of REC vs non-REC within each gene x compartment.

Code 
baseline_stats <- draws_df |>
  mutate(model = recode(model, !!!model_labels)) |>
  group_by(gene, model) |>
  summarise(
    baseline_mean_log_mu = mean(baseline_log_mu),
    baseline_sd_log_mu = sd(baseline_log_mu),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

cohort_projection <- cohort_tests |>
  inner_join(baseline_stats, by = "gene", relationship = "many-to-many") |>
  mutate(
    signed_z = (cohort_log_mu - baseline_mean_log_mu) / baseline_sd_log_mu,
    abs_z = abs(signed_z)
  )

cohort_projection |>
  select(
    gene, model, cohort, cohort_log_mu, baseline_mean_log_mu,
    baseline_sd_log_mu, signed_z, abs_z
  ) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))) |>
  arrange(gene, model, cohort)
Code 
recurrence_margin <- cohort_projection |>
  select(gene, compartment, recurrence, model, abs_z) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = recurrence, values_from = abs_z) |>
  mutate(
    margin_rec_minus_nonrec = REC - `non-REC`,
    rec_farther_from_healthy = margin_rec_minus_nonrec > 0
  )

recurrence_margin |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))) |>
  arrange(gene, compartment, model)

A positive margin_rec_minus_nonrec means the REC cohort is farther from the healthy baseline than the non-REC cohort — the direction the HCC case study predicts. Summarising across all gene x compartment comparisons:

Code 
baseline_choice <- recurrence_margin |>
  group_by(model) |>
  summarise(
    n_comparisons = n(),
    n_rec_farther = sum(rec_farther_from_healthy),
    frac_rec_farther = mean(rec_farther_from_healthy),
    mean_margin_sd = mean(margin_rec_minus_nonrec),
    median_margin_sd = median(margin_rec_minus_nonrec),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(n_rec_farther), desc(mean_margin_sd))

baseline_choice
Code 
best <- baseline_choice |> slice(1)
re_row <- baseline_choice |> filter(model == "Random effect")
int_row <- baseline_choice |> filter(model == "Interaction")

cat(glue(
  "Across {re_row$n_comparisons} gene x compartment comparisons, the ",
  "**{re_row$model}** baseline recovers the expected REC-farther-from-healthy ",
  "ordering in {re_row$n_rec_farther}/{re_row$n_comparisons} cases with a mean ",
  "REC - non-REC separation of {round(re_row$mean_margin_sd, 2)} baseline SD, ",
  "versus {int_row$n_rec_farther}/{int_row$n_comparisons} and ",
  "{round(int_row$mean_margin_sd, 2)} SD for the {int_row$model} baseline. ",
  "On this case-study criterion the **{best$model}** baseline is preferred."
))

Across 8 gene x compartment comparisons, the Random effect baseline recovers the expected REC-farther-from-healthy ordering in 8/8 cases with a mean REC - non-REC separation of 1.19 baseline SD, versus 7/8 and 0.42 SD for the Interaction baseline. On this case-study criterion the Random effect baseline is preferred.

Why the random-effect baseline wins here. The two formulas place the healthy liver mean in a broadly similar location, but the interaction baseline is roughly twice as wide (see the SD comparison above). Because the cohort projections are fixed, a wider baseline compresses every standardized distance toward zero, shrinking the REC vs non-REC separation and even flipping the sign in the weakest comparison. Partial pooling in the random-effect model yields a tighter, better-identified liver reference that keeps recurrent cohorts cleanly outside the healthy envelope — exactly the behaviour the HCC proximity score relies on. The interaction alternative does not add case-study value at liver n = 71; its extra flexibility mostly buys uncertainty.

Interpretation

Code 
n_genes <- nrow(comparison)
mean_abs_diff <- mean(comparison$abs_diff_mean_log_mu)
mean_corr <- mean(comparison$corr_draws, na.rm = TRUE)
int_wider <- all(comparison$sd_log_mu_int > comparison$sd_log_mu_re)

cat(glue(
  "Across {n_genes} genes, the mean absolute difference in comprehensive liver log(μ) is {round(mean_abs_diff, 2)}. ",
  "Mean draw-wise correlation between formulas is {round(mean_corr, 2)}. ",
  if (int_wider) {
    "The interaction model produces wider baseline uncertainty for every gene, consistent with overparameterisation when liver n = 71."
  } else {
    "Baseline uncertainty differs by gene between formulas."
  }
))

Across 4 genes, the mean absolute difference in comprehensive liver log(μ) is 0.53. Mean draw-wise correlation between formulas is -0.01. The interaction model produces wider baseline uncertainty for every gene, consistent with overparameterisation when liver n = 71.

Random-effect model (current pipeline). Liver tissue intercepts and slopes are partially pooled toward a population mean informed largely by blood. This reduces variance but can bias liver estimates toward the dominant tissue when liver-specific signal is weak.

Interaction model (pilot). Liver is estimated without shrinkage, but requires many tissue × covariate coefficients. With 21 tissues and sparse liver age/sex/ethnicity combinations, fits can become unstable (wider baselines, lower concordance with the RE reference).

Implication for HCC. If the two formulas disagree materially on liver healthy μ, healthy-proximity scores will shift even when patient pseudobulk is unchanged. This pilot quantifies that discrepancy before committing to a formula change. A lighter compromise — e.g. fixed liver intercept with RE slopes elsewhere — may be worth exploring if liver-specific bias under RE is confirmed in downstream HCC ranking tests.
